outcome: No source I could open shows that infinitely many Kynea primes have been proved or disproved, and I found no event since 26 January 2024 that bears on the base-2 question; the only in-window activity is computer searches that add further exponents, including one in a different (base-10) family.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many n for which the Kynea number (2^n+1)^2 - 2 = 4^n + 2^(n+1) - 1 is prime? The statement as frozen does not define 'Kynea prime'. Wikipedia's Kynea number article, OEIS A091514 and MathWorld use this base-2 definition, and it is the reading used here. Part 1: infinitude of the set of such n. The statement asks for nothing else (no count, no density, no structure of the set). Alternative reading, recorded for the later pass: the Prime-Wiki project (rieselprime.de) calls (b*n+1)^2 - 2 a Kynea prime for each base b; on that reading the question is one about infinitely many n for each base, and a base-10 find (event propper-2024-base10) would be an instance of a different family.

events.what_happened: Amelia Carolina Sparavigna (Politecnico di Torino) posted on Zenodo 'Binary Operators of the Groupoids of OEIS A093112 and A093069 Numbers (Carol and Kynea Numbers)', studying binary operators on the Carol and Kynea number sets and linking them to Mersenne and Fermat integers. The same author's later Zenodo and International Journal of Sciences papers (Oct 2019) cover related groupoids including Kynea numbers.
events.revisions: Zenodo record v1, 6 June 2019 (per the record page). Later Zenodo papers by the same author dated 3 Oct 2019 and an IJSci paper Oct 2019 are separate works.
events.delivers: Nothing about primes. It concerns algebraic groupoid operators on the Kynea number set (the integers (2^n+1)^2 - 2, not necessarily prime). It does not address whether infinitely many of them are prime.
events.remains: The whole problem: whether infinitely many Kynea numbers are prime.
events.direction: Neutral to the question: it studies the Kynea numbers as a set with operators and says nothing about primality.

events.what_happened: Mark Rodenkirch's base-2 Kynea prime (2^661478 + 1)^2 - 2, with 398,250 decimal digits. PrimePages lists it as submitted 18 June 2016, proved prime by PFGW 3.7.7 N-1/N+1 (Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge) test, proof code p393 credited to Rodenkirch, CKSieve and OpenPFGW. OEIS A091513 credits the term 661478 (a(51)) to Rodenkirch, added 19 June 2016. Prime-Wiki's base-2 log records the same find as 2016-06-18.
events.revisions: PrimePages submission 2016-06-18; OEIS extension note says a(51) added 19 June 2016. The one-day difference is noted; the PrimePages date is taken as the first record.
events.delivers: One more base-2 Kynea prime, at index 661478. It is one instance of the family and says nothing about whether there are infinitely many. Under the 'one more instance of an existential family' reading it moves the known-instance count only.
events.remains: The whole problem: whether infinitely many n give a prime (2^n+1)^2 - 2.

machine_checked.system: PFGW 3.7.7 (GWNUM 27.11), N-1/N+1 Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge primality proof, proof code p393

events.directly_checkable: The number itself can be re-tested with a PFGW-style primality prover; PrimePages records the command pfgw64 -tc -q"(2^661478+1)^2-2" and reports the test as proved. I did not re-run it.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem: a further instance of the family being prime. It does not bear on infinitude.
events.object: The base-2 Kynea prime (2^661478+1)^2 - 2, a 398,250-digit prime found by computer search and proved by a Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge (N-1/N+1) certificate. Explicit, not non-constructive; it is a found instance, not a proof of anything general.

ai.disclosed_cost: PrimePages records a run of about 6.72 hours on a 4c+4c 3.5 GHz Xeon machine.

events.what_happened: Prime-Wiki's base-2 Carol/Kynea page logs 'Found n = 852770, Ryan Propper' on 2019-07-14, under the combined history for both types. The Wikipedia Kynea number article (read as a summary) and the search snippets say this index gives the largest known Kynea prime, (2^852770+1)^2 - 2, with 513,419 digits, found with CKSieve and PrimeFormGW. The Prime-Wiki log does not say which of the two families the index belongs to; the Wikipedia Carol number mirror instead gives Carol's largest index as 695631 (Rodenkirch, 2016). OEIS A091513 as cached does not list 852770 (its last term is 661478).
events.delivers: One more instance at index 852770, if it is a Kynea prime. Like the 2016 find it adds one instance and does not bear on infinitude.
events.doubts: The attribution of index 852770 to the Kynea family rather than Carol is unresolved in the sources I could read. The Prime-Wiki base-2 page, which would settle it, returned HTTP 503 each time I tried to open it. The 513,419-digit figure comes from a Wikipedia summary, not a PrimePages entry I could open.
events.direction: As for the 2016 find: one further instance, not a bound or a proof.
events.object: Possibly the base-2 Kynea prime (2^852770+1)^2 - 2, 513,419 digits, found by computer search. Attribution to Kynea rather than Carol is not confirmed from a primary source I could open.

events.what_happened: Prime-Wiki's base-10 Carol/Kynea page, as shown in a search snippet, logs 'Found n = 2332974, Ryan Propper', dated 2024-02-20, for the generalised form (10n+1)^2 - 2. events.delivers: Nothing toward the base-2 problem. It is an instance of a different family ((10n+1)^2 - 2, base 10), so under the scope rule it is a different question. If the later pass reads the Prime-Wiki naming as the problem, it is one further instance of a base-10 family, which still does not move infinitude.

events.doubts: Based on a search snippet only; the page could not be opened.
events.direction: Neutral: an instance in a different family.

disputes.summary: Whether index 852770 (found 2019-07-14 by Ryan Propper) is a base-2 Kynea prime or a Carol prime. Prime-Wiki's log puts it under 'both types'; the Wikipedia Kynea article says Kynea; the Wikipedia Carol mirror gives Carol's largest index as 695631, so the sources do not settle it.

Largest known base-2 Kynea index: OEIS A091513 as cached gives 661478 (June 2016, Rodenkirch) as its last term, and its b-file stops at n=51. The Wikipedia Kynea article and Prime-Wiki give 852770 (2019). The OEIS cache may predate the 2019 entry; it was not refreshed in my fetch.

summary: The problem is whether infinitely many n make (2^n+1)^2 - 2 = 4^n + 2^(n+1) - 1 prime. I found no source saying this has been proved, disproved, or moved toward. Wikipedia's Kynea number article, as read through a summary fetch, places the Kynea numbers among unsolved problems; the Wikipedia list's own bullet was not reached in the portion of the page I read (I read roughly the first 200,000 of 294,882 characters, and the number-theory bullets sit in the rest). The Carol number mirror says the infinitude of Carol primes is unsolved. The problem is treated as open in every source I read, with no source claiming progress. The literature I could find on Kynea primes is almost entirely computational and reference material: OEIS A091513/A091514, MathWorld's near-square page and its Kynea stub, PrimePages records (t5k.org pages 121686, 85906, 121801 and 1073807359), and Prime-Wiki tables (which are not current for me; the pages returned HTTP 503 each time I tried them). Within the window (26 Jan 2024 onward) the only record I found is a base-10 find in Prime-Wiki's family (2024-02-20), which is a different family and not an event on the base-2 problem; Prime-Wiki's base-b families of 2023 (bases 36, 666, 1484, 2634) and a base-302 entry with a March 2025 update are finds or checks in other bases, which I did not open and did not record as events. Pre-window events recorded are the 2016 (n=661478) and 2019 (n=852770) base-2 finds, which are instances and not progress toward infinitude, and a 2019 Sparavigna paper on Carol/Kynea groupoids that does not address primality. Close call on scope: the base-b Prime-Wiki usage of 'Kynea prime' could make the 2024 base-10 find, and the many base-b finds, count as 'Kynea primes' for the problem; I have recorded only the base-10 find as an event and left the rest as noted. AI search: I searched for Kynea primes with AI terms (AlphaEvolve, OpenAI, DeepMind, ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini, AI-generated proof, LLM) and found nothing linking any system to Kynea primes. The AI-related results I did see (AlphaEvolve's 67-problem paper, an OpenAI prime-gap claim, Axiom Math's 246-prime-gap formalization, a 2023 ChatGPT-on-conjecture episode) are about other problems and are not recorded as events. All prime records found were by distributed or personal computer searches (PFGW, CKSieve, PrimeFormGW), not AI.
competing_reading: Read the Prime-Wiki usage: 'Kynea prime' means (b*n+1)^2 - 2 for any base b, and the problem asks about each base. On that reading there are many open families, and the 2023-2025 base-b finds (for example bases 36, 666, 1484, 2634, 302) are events that move exponent lists in those families. That is a broader reading than the Wikipedia definition the record uses, and it would change the event count but not the answer that infinitude is open for every family.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A current copy of the Prime-Wiki base-2 Carol/Kynea page with its full history, to fix the 852770 attribution and any post-2020 entry. (2) The OEIS A091513 b-file and extension history after 2019. (3) The MersenneForum Carol/Kynea search thread, which the Prime-Wiki says now coordinates the search. (4) The Wikipedia list's number-theory bullet and its link target (the bullets lie in the unread final part of the page). (5) Hibbs (2022) p. 33 via ProQuest. (6) A literature search of zbMATH and MathSciNet for 'Kynea' (zbMATH returned HTTP 403 in my attempt). (7) Any 2024-2026 arXiv paper using 'Kynea' or 'Carol-Kynea' in its title or abstract; my arXiv searches returned zero results for 'Kynea' and for 'Carol number OR Kynea'.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many Kynea primes exist. Individual prime finds (2016, 2019) are finitely many instances and settle nothing; the 2024 base-10 find concerns (10^n+1)^2-2, a different family under the standard base-2 definition, so it is a variant (and even under the Prime-Wiki base-b reading it would only be an instance). Sparavigna's groupoid paper and the unread Hibbs thesis bear on the topic without settling or bounding anything. No AI involvement was found in any event.
judgement.doubts: Prime-Wiki pages were unreachable, so post-2019 base-2 finds (if any) could not be checked; any such find would still be an instance only. The Hibbs thesis content is unknown.
